reactions.title: Hydrogen burns in oxygen
reactions.conditionLabel: Ignition of a hydrogen–oxygen mixture; conceptual example
observations: Heat and flame accompany rapid combustion.
An ignited gas mixture can give a loud report; the blast symbol is qualitative.
Water first forms as vapor and can condense on cooling.
reactions.explanation: Hydrogen and oxygen atoms rearrange into water molecules. Ignition is required in this model; a mixture alone is not a prediction of immediate combustion.

reactions.title: Magnesium forms an oxide
reactions.conditionLabel: Ignited magnesium in oxygen; simplified oxygen-only chemistry
observations: Bright light accompanies burning.
Solid magnesium oxide forms.
reactions.explanation: The metal combines with molecular oxygen. This oxygen-only model omits side reactions possible when magnesium burns in air.

reactions.title: Iron and sulfur form a compound
reactions.conditionLabel: Thermal activation of an iron–sulfur mixture
observations: A red glow travels through the reacting mixture.
Iron(II) sulfide is formed.
reactions.explanation: A mixture becomes a compound after activation. The S₈ formula represents elemental sulfur, so eight iron atoms are needed per sulfur molecule.

reactions.title: Complete combustion of carbon
reactions.conditionLabel: Ignition with sufficient oxygen; complete combustion model
observations: Carbon dioxide gas is formed; it is not colored smoke.
reactions.explanation: This models complete combustion only. Oxygen-limited conditions can produce other products and are outside this scenario.

reactions.title: Light initiates hydrogen chloride formation
reactions.conditionLabel: Photochemical activation by suitable light; conceptual hazardous gas mixture
observations: A light-initiated gas reaction can be explosive.
Toxicity warning: the chlorine-containing gas mixture presents an inhalation hazard.
reactions.explanation: Suitable light can initiate a rapid chain reaction producing hydrogen chloride gas. The warning concerns chemical exposure, not radioactivity. This is a conceptual demonstration only.

reactions.title: Sodium and chlorine form salt
reactions.conditionLabel: Ignited sodium in chlorine; conceptual demonstration
observations: A yellow flame accompanies reaction.
White sodium chloride particles form; these are solid aerosol, not steam.
Chlorine reactant is toxic by inhalation.
reactions.explanation: The product has very different properties from the elements. Sodium chloride is a compound with equal numbers of sodium and chlorine atoms.

reactions.title: Sodium reacts with water
reactions.conditionLabel: Contact with liquid water; conceptual aqueous reaction
observations: Energy is released and hydrogen gas is produced.
Sodium hydroxide remains in solution.
reactions.explanation: Sodium displaces hydrogen from water. Flame is not an automatic effect: the source notes that hydrogen only sometimes burns.

reactions.title: Magnesium releases hydrogen from acid
reactions.conditionLabel: Magnesium in dilute aqueous hydrochloric acid
observations: Hydrogen bubbles form while magnesium is consumed.
reactions.explanation: Magnesium replaces hydrogen in the acid; magnesium chloride remains dissolved. Gas formation does not mean that boiling or combustion occurred.

reactions.title: Zinc releases hydrogen from acid
reactions.conditionLabel: Zinc surface in aqueous hydrochloric acid
observations: Hydrogen gas bubbles form as zinc reacts.
reactions.explanation: The metal is converted into dissolved zinc chloride. The equation describes the chemical change without predicting its speed.

reactions.title: Acid and base neutralize
reactions.conditionLabel: Dilute aqueous acid and base; stoichiometric neutralization
observations: The solution warms.
Sodium chloride stays dissolved; no salt precipitate is modeled.
reactions.explanation: Hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions form water. Sodium and chloride ions remain in solution as spectator ions. Heat release alone does not imply flame or steam.

reactions.title: Bicarbonate and acid release carbon dioxide
reactions.conditionLabel: Aqueous bicarbonate and hydrochloric acid
observations: Fizzing shows carbon dioxide gas leaving the solution.
reactions.explanation: Acid reacts with bicarbonate to form water and carbon dioxide; sodium chloride remains dissolved. The gas is not water vapor.

reactions.title: A blue precipitate appears
reactions.conditionLabel: Dilute aqueous solutions at room temperature; precipitation stage without excess concentrated alkali
observations: Blue copper(II) hydroxide precipitates.
reactions.explanation: Copper ions combine with hydroxide ions to form an insoluble solid. Sodium and sulfate ions remain dissolved. Heating and strongly concentrated excess alkali are outside this model.

reactions.title: Copper displaces silver
reactions.conditionLabel: Copper in aqueous silver nitrate
observations: Silver deposits on the copper surface over time.
reactions.explanation: Copper transfers electrons to silver ions. Metallic silver forms while copper enters solution as copper(II) ions; nitrate ions are spectators.

reactions.title: Helium and neon remain a mixture
reactions.conditionLabel: Ordinary room conditions; no plasma, electrical excitation, or extreme pressure
observations: No chemical reaction is modeled under these stated conditions.
The gases remain a mixture.
reactions.explanation: Helium and neon are exceptionally unreactive noble gases. This claim is restricted to ordinary conditions, not exotic high-energy or high-pressure chemistry.
